assessment.nobel_worthiness: A clear observational discovery of a new window on the universe: a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, with a long instrumental programme (kilometre-scale ice Cherenkov detection) that made it possible. It identifies messengers from cosmic accelerators and later source associations, which is the kind of finding that nature itself delivers.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led the IceCube concept and the science programme; Karle and Spiering are credited as leaders of the construction and the analyses that established the signal. The collaboration is large, so a three-person split is a simplification, and some contributors from precursors (AMANDA, Baikal) are not in the credited names.
assessment.maturity: The astrophysical flux has been confirmed repeatedly with independent channels and now has source evidence (e.g. the blazar and Galactic-plane results). The interpretation of individual sources is still developing, but the discovery itself is stable and timely.
uncertainties: Whether the prize should reward the detector concept, the 2013 discovery or the source identification is not settled.
Credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the precursor experiments could be disputed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, followed by experimental realization in HgTe quantum wells, opened a major field and reshaped understanding of band topology and edge transport. Theory and experiment are tightly linked.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical proposals; Molenkamp led the experimental observation (with the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal as an important intermediate step that is not among the credited names). The three-person configuration is plausible but leaves out the BHZ prediction and the 3D materials work.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation in many materials and a vast follow-up literature; the 2016 prize covered topological phases and transitions in a different sense, so this is complementary rather than duplicative. Timing is good.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2016 prize and with the BHZ and 3D topological insulator contributions complicates attribution.
Practical impact is still modest relative to the conceptual impact.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cirac and Zoller proposed the trapped-ion quantum gate and later the schemes for analogue and digital quantum simulation with cold atoms and ions, providing the blueprint for the physical implementation of quantum computation. Their ideas have been realized experimentally and underpin a large community.
assessment.attribution: The two-person credit is clean: the 1995 Cirac-Zoller gate proposal and subsequent joint and individual work are well established as theirs. Experimental realizations by others (Wineland group, Blatt, Monroe) were partly recognized in 2012.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally confirmed over decades across several platforms; the field is mature, though large-scale quantum advantage remains in progress. Recognition is plausible and not premature.
uncertainties: Part of the experimental follow-up was already recognized in 2012, so the committee may see the theory-only prize as incomplete.
Boundaries to Rydberg and optical-lattice quantum simulation are blurry.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Theoretical prediction of flat bands at magic angles and the 2018 observation of correlated insulating and superconducting phases in twisted bilayer graphene created the field of moire quantum matter, with a fast-growing set of tunable strongly correlated phenomena.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald supplied the decisive 2011 theory; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the experimental discovery. Other groups (e.g. Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov) made essential independent observations and could challenge a narrow trio.
assessment.maturity: Replicated by many groups, though the field is under 10 years old and the nature of the superconductivity and correlated states is not fully settled. Fairly timely but arguably early.
uncertainties: Microscopic mechanism of superconductivity remains debated.
Credit among experimental groups and Kim, Fal'ko and others is not fully resolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, based on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, deliver unprecedented stability and accuracy and enable tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. A strong instrumental discovery with clear lasting impact on metrology.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and Ye drove the clocks to record precision; the two-person credit is natural. Hall and Hansch were honoured in 2005 for the comb, and Wineland in 2012, so this is a natural continuation.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent lab realizations and international comparisons confirm it; the redefinition of the second is under discussion. Mature and timely.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier prizes on laser spectroscopy and ion clocks.
Contributions of other groups (Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow) not in the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Precision mapping of CMB anisotropies by WMAP and Planck fixed the parameters of the Lambda-CDM model and delivered a cornerstone of modern cosmology. It is a central observational foundation for any theory work on inflation and dark energy.
assessment.attribution: Bennett led WMAP, Page and Spergel contributed key instrument and theory/analysis roles. Puget and the Planck leadership, plus COBE (2006 prize) and the earlier ground-based experiments, complicate a fair configuration.
assessment.maturity: Extremely mature and confirmed by independent missions; the 2006 prize already covered the blackbody and first anisotropies, so precision cosmology is a second step that may be seen as incremental.
uncertainties: Allocation among WMAP, Planck and the ground-based experiments is difficult.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of fast radio bursts opened a new class of extragalactic radio transients, now used as probes of baryons in the intergalactic medium. A surprising observational discovery, though the sources are not fully understood.
assessment.attribution: Lorimer and McLaughlin found the original burst in archival data; Bailes was a co-author and later led the localization and cosmological work. Others (CHIME, ASKAP, Thornton et al., Spitler et al.) were also decisive for establishing the phenomenon as real and extragalactic.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed with thousands of bursts and a magnetar association, but the progenitor and emission mechanism are still open. Somewhat early.
uncertainties: Origin of the bursts is not settled.
Credit split between the 2007 discovery and later localization and CHIME work is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The first horizon-scale images of M87* and Sgr A* directly test strong-field gravity and black-hole accretion physics, making a very concrete observational anchor for black-hole physics, which sits close to my own subject area.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed imaging the shadow and Doeleman led the VLBI development and the EHT collaboration; Moran's earlier VLBI work is also important. The result is a very large collaboration, so a person-level attribution is difficult and subject to the Nobel statutes.
assessment.maturity: Results confirmed by repeated epochs and a second source, but interpretation (spin, jet launching, tests of GR) is still maturing. Relatively recent, but impact is broad.
uncertainties: Large-collaboration attribution is difficult under the three-person limit.
Systematics and model dependence of the image interpretation remain under study.
